documents.title: Putting a language model in front of Active Directory access requests, with me as the approval step
Predicting delivery time with linear regression, and what feature elimination cost me
What 490,000 New York taxi trips say about when drivers actually earn
Keep a human approval step between the language model and Active Directory
Leave a senior IT operations role for an MSc in AI
Build the eval harness before the chat interface
The seven questions I get asked, and my actual answers

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
I was handling 50 or more incidents a day in ServiceNow as a senior analyst on IT support, and
a steady share of them were access requests: an account to create, a group membership to
change, a permission to revoke. Each one was individually trivial and collectively expensive.
The work was reading a ticket written in prose, deciding what directory change it was actually
asking for, and then making that change correctly.

The slow part was not the change. It was the reading and the translating.

## Constraints

Three that shaped everything:

1. **Directory changes are destructive and auditable.** Removing the wrong group membership
   locks someone out of their job. There is no undo that leaves no trace.
2. **I had no mandate to automate anyone's work but my own.** This was a tool I built for my
   own queue, not a team initiative with a sponsor.
3. **Enterprise environment.** I could use the internal model the company provided, not an
   external API, and what I can say about the internals here is limited by the
   confidentiality terms I am still bound by. So this describes my approach and my results
   rather than their systems.

## Options I considered

**Keep doing it by hand.** The honest baseline. Reliable, and the cost was my attention rather
than any risk.

**Script it with no model.** Parse the ticket with rules and regular expressions. This fails on
the actual problem, which is that people describe access requests in wildly inconsistent prose.
A rule set that handles that variation becomes a worse version of a language model.

**Let it run unattended.** The script reads the ticket, decides, and applies the change with no
human in the loop. Fastest, and I rejected it. An LLM misreading a prose request and then
writing that misreading into a live directory is not a risk worth the minutes it saves, and I
would not have been able to defend the decision if it had gone wrong once.

sections.heading: What I chose
sections.content:
A Python tool that read the ticket, used the internal model to turn the prose into a concrete
proposed change, and then presented that proposal to me for approval. I checked it and applied
it. The model never touched the directory.

The design principle was that the model does the interpretation, which is what it is good at,
and I do the authorisation, which is what I was accountable for.

## What happened

It saved me roughly 2 to 5 hours a week. That is the interpretation and drafting step, not the
approval, which I still did on every single request.

Two things it did not do. It never gained a second user: I built it for my own queue and never
packaged it for anyone else. And it stopped running when I left the company in December 2025,
because it had exactly one owner and no handover.

## What I would do differently

**It had no owner but me, and that is a design failure, not an accident of the exit.** A tool
that saves a few hours a week is worth documenting and handing over. I never wrote down how it
worked, never sat with a colleague to get them using it, and never asked whether the team
wanted it. So the value ended on my last day, which means the honest accounting of its impact
is two and a half years of my own time and nothing beyond that.

**I did not measure how often it was right.** The approval step means I saw every proposal, so I
had a free labelled dataset sitting in front of me every day: what the model proposed against
what I actually applied. Logging that would have told me the acceptance rate, which kinds of
request it misread, and whether the gap was closing. I would then have had an evidenced answer
to "could this run unattended?" instead of an instinct. That is the same mistake as shipping a
model without an eval set, and I made it before I knew that was the name for it.

That lesson is the direct ancestor of this assistant, which measures its retrieval quality
against a golden set before anything else gets built.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Predict how long a food delivery order will take, from the order itself and the state of the
courier fleet at the moment it was placed. The dataset had 175,777 orders across 15 columns:
market, order protocol, basket composition, item prices, and three fleet-state counts, with a
pickup and a delivery timestamp.

## Constraints

This was a graded assignment on the IIIT Bangalore Data Science programme, and the brief fixed
the model to linear regression. That mattered. It meant I could not answer "is a linear model
right for this?" by trying a non-linear one, so every real decision I made was about the data
and the features rather than the algorithm.

## What I did

The target did not exist in the data. I derived `time_taken` from the gap between the pickup
and delivery timestamps, then pulled `order_hour` and `isWeekend` out of the order timestamp,
and computed a `distance` feature. That gave 12 usable features.

I split 80/20 before any cleaning: 140,621 training rows and 35,156 test rows. Outliers went
next, using boxplots to see them and the interquartile range to remove them, which took the
training set from 140,621 to 139,242 rows. Just under 1%.

Then I fitted the model twice. Once on all 12 features, and once on 8 chosen by Recursive
Feature Elimination, which is the approach the brief pointed at.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.content:
All numbers below are on the held-out test set.

| Model | Features | MAE (min) | RMSE | R² |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All features | 12 | 2.33 | 3.24 | 0.8800 |
| RFE, unscaled | 8 | 2.95 | 3.98 | 0.8191 |
| RFE, scaled | 8 | 2.45 | 3.24 | 0.8737 |

**Feature elimination made the model worse.** Dropping four features cost six points of R² and
half a minute of mean absolute error. I had gone in assuming the opposite, which is the useful
part: the assignment framed RFE as a refinement step, and on this data it was a downgrade.

The second row against the third is the part I would want to be asked about. Ordinary least
squares is scale-invariant, so standardising the inputs cannot change R². The two rows differ
because RFE ran on the scaled and unscaled matrices separately and **selected different
features**:

- unscaled: `market_id`, `order_protocol`, `num_distinct_items`, `total_onshift_dashers`,
  `total_outstanding_orders`, `distance`, `order_hour`, `isWeekend`
- scaled: `market_id`, `order_protocol`, `subtotal`, `total_onshift_dashers`,
  `total_busy_dashers`, `total_outstanding_orders`, `distance`, `order_hour`

Swapping `num_distinct_items` and `isWeekend` for `subtotal` and `total_busy_dashers` is what
recovered five of the six lost points. So the honest reading is not "scaling helped." It is
"RFE is unstable on correlated features, and the selection it produced on the scaled matrix
happened to be better." A second courier-load feature beat a weekend flag.

Fleet state carried real signal. Three of the eight surviving features in both runs were
courier counts, which fits the intuition that delivery time is mostly about how busy the fleet
is rather than what was ordered.

sections.heading: What I would do differently
sections.content:
Fit a gradient-boosted baseline alongside it. Not to submit, but to find out what the linear
assumption cost. Without that number I cannot say whether R² 0.88 is good or whether a tree
model would have reached 0.95 on the same features, and that is the first thing anyone
technical will ask. The brief fixing the model is a reason I did not do it during the
assignment, not a reason it should stay undone.

I would also stop treating RFE as a step you apply. On this data it needed a sweep across
feature counts with the scores plotted, which would have shown the drop immediately instead of
leaving me to find it a year later.

## Correction

The written answers in the submitted notebook describe a different dataset. They name columns
such as `Discount_offered`, `Weight_in_gms` and `Warehouse_block`, which belong to a retail
shipping dataset and do not appear in this data, and one answer still carries a "replace with
the actual column name" placeholder. The code and the metrics are sound. The prose on top of
them was not reviewed, and it is being rewritten against the actual heatmap and coefficient
output.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Work out when and where New York taxi demand actually is, from the city's own 2023 yellow cab
trip records, and turn that into something a dispatcher could act on. A single month of those
records is 3,014,248 trips across 22 columns, so the first problem is that the data does not
fit comfortably in memory on a laptop.

## Constraints

A graded assignment on the IIIT Bangalore programme, with a stated target of keeping the
working set near 250,000 to 300,000 rows. Local machine, no cluster. That forced the sampling
decision up front rather than letting me defer it.

## What I did

I sampled across all twelve months of 2023 rather than taking one month whole, which keeps
seasonal variation in the data, and landed at 489,542 trips. Then the cleaning, which took
longer than the analysis:

- Dropped `vendorid` and `store_and_fwd_flag` as unusable for the questions I had.
- Investigated negative fares before removing them, broken down by rate code, because a
  negative fare is usually a refund rather than an error and I wanted to know which.
- Filtered zero and negative values across fare, tip, total and distance.
- Bounded trip duration to between 1 and 180 minutes, distance to under 50 miles, and
  passenger count to 1 to 6. Each of those cut a tail that would otherwise have dominated the
  averages.
- Joined the trips to the city's taxi zone shapefile through `LocationID` so pickups and
  dropoffs became places rather than integers.

sections.heading: What I found
sections.content:
**Tipping is about when and how, not how far.** Tip percentages are highest between 10pm and
2am, and card payments tip substantially more than cash. That is the finding I would lead
with, because it points at driver earnings rather than company revenue, and the action it
implies costs nothing: a driver choosing between a late shift and an early one has a reason to
pick the late one.

Demand moves through the day in a shape a dispatcher can use. Mornings load from the outer
residential zones into Midtown and the Financial District; evenings reverse it; late Friday and
Saturday nights concentrate in the nightlife zones; the 3am to 6am window is airport traffic
and shift workers. The top ten pickup and dropoff zones, the pickup-to-dropoff ratio per zone,
and night-hour pickup concentration are all computed directly from the trip records.

Fare per mile is not flat. Comparing vendors across three distance tiers, under 2 miles, 2 to 5,
and over 5, short trips earn far more per mile than long ones, which is what you would expect
from a fixed base fare and why long airport runs are less attractive than they look.

## What I would do differently

**Three figures in my submitted notebook are plotted from random numbers.** The starter template
seeded the zone trip counts with `np.random.randint(0, 100, len(zones))` and the route speeds
with `np.random.uniform(20, 60, ...)` as scaffolding to demonstrate the plotting calls, and I
never replaced them with real counts. A later cell then divides those random numbers by the
sampling fraction to "scale up to the full population", which scales up noise. So the trips-per-
zone choropleth and the slowest-routes analysis carry no information, and the congestion
recommendation that depended on them is withdrawn. The zone findings above come from the
value-count work, which is real. I found this on review, months after submitting, and it is the
most useful thing this project taught me: a figure that renders is not a figure that is right.

My two conclusion cells also contradict each other on peak hours, one saying 1pm to 9pm and the
other 7am to 9am and 5pm to 7pm. I did not reconcile them at the time, which means at least one
was written from impression rather than from the plot.

The conclusions themselves sit inside triple-quoted strings in code cells, so they do not render
as text. The best part of the work is nearly invisible to anyone reading the notebook.

And the recommendations need numbers. "Raise peak fares 10 to 15%" is an opinion until it comes
with an estimated revenue effect, and the data could have supported that estimate. A
recommendation without a number is not an analysis result.

Finally, I would test whether the filtering shaped the findings. Removing trips over 180 minutes
and over 50 miles is defensible, but those are exactly the trips that matter most to a driver
deciding whether to take an airport run. I should have run the headline findings once with the
bounds and once without and reported whether they held.

sections.heading: Context
sections.content:
Access requests arrived as prose in ServiceNow tickets: create this account, add
this person to that group, revoke this permission. Reading the ticket and working
out which concrete directory change it was asking for took most of the time. The
change itself took seconds.

A language model is good at exactly that translation step, and I had an internal
one available. The question was how much authority to give it.

## Decision

The model proposes, I approve, the script applies. The model never touched the
directory directly.

## Alternatives considered

**Unattended end to end.** The script reads the ticket, decides, and makes the
change. This saves the most time and I rejected it. Directory writes are
destructive and audited, and a wrong group removal locks someone out of their job
with no clean undo. I would also have had no answer if it had gone wrong once.

**Rules and regular expressions, no model.** Fails on the actual problem. People
describe access requests in wildly inconsistent prose, and a rule set broad enough
to cover that variation becomes a worse language model.

## Consequences

It saved 2 to 5 hours a week of my own time, which was the interpretation step
rather than the approval step. I stayed accountable for every change, which was
the point.

What I did not see at the time: the approval step was a free labelled dataset. I
saw every proposal next to what I actually applied, every day, and logged none of
it. With that log I could have reported an acceptance rate, found which request
types it misread, and answered "could this run unattended?" with evidence instead
of instinct. I was shipping a model with no eval set, before I knew that was the
name for the mistake.

sections.heading: Context
sections.content:
By 2025 I was a Senior Analyst at Capgemini, two and a half years in, running 50
or more incidents a day against SLA and administering Active Directory and
endpoint compliance across enterprise environments. The role was stable and I was
good at it.

Two things had changed underneath that. I had been studying through the IIIT
Bangalore Data Science programme alongside the job, which finished with the NLP
specialisation in October 2025, so the interest was two years old rather than
sudden. And I had built the access-request tool described in
[001](001-human-approval-before-directory-writes.md). That tool was the first
time the work felt like engineering a system rather than operating one, and I
wanted considerably more of that than the role contained.

## Decision

Resign in December 2025 and move to London for an MSc in Artificial Intelligence
and Computer Science at Northeastern University London.

## Alternatives considered

**Stay and move internally.** Capgemini is large and has ML work in it. The
honest reason I did not pursue this: internal moves from operations into
engineering are slow and usually need the credential I did not have. I would have
spent two years waiting for permission.

**Keep studying part time and stay employed.** Cheaper and lower risk, and it is
what I had already been doing for two years. It had produced certificates rather
than shipped systems, which told me the constraint was time and not motivation.

**Self-study and apply directly.** No tuition, no visa cost, no relocation. I
rejected it because I had no production ML to point at, and without either a
credential or a portfolio the applications go nowhere. The MSc buys the
credential; this assistant is meant to be the portfolio half.

sections.heading: Consequences
sections.content:
The cost is real: a salary given up, tuition, and a student visa that permits
20 hours a week in term time rather than full-time work until the course
completes in May 2027.

What it buys is time to build things that can be measured, and a dissertation in
agentic AI and LLMs that sits on the same ground as the work I want to be hired
for. The thing I am still exposed to is the obvious one: three years of
production operations is not three years of production ML, and I say so rather
than blur it.

sections.heading: Context
sections.content:
This assistant is a retrieval system with a chat box on the front. The chat box
is the part anyone can see and the part I most wanted to build. The retrieval
quality is the part that decides whether anything it says is true.

The phase order I am following puts corpus and ingestion first, then a retrieval
pipeline where every option is a config flag, then the eval harness, then an
ablation study across those flags, and only then the chat interface. Chat is
phase five of ten.

## Decision

No chat interface until the golden set, the retrieval metrics and the
faithfulness judge exist and produce numbers.

## Alternatives considered

**Chat first, evaluate later.** The natural order, and the one I wanted. It fails
for a specific reason rather than a moral one: once a chat UI exists, retrieval
gets tuned by asking it questions and seeing whether the answers feel right.
Feeling right is not a measurement, it does not survive a change to the chunking
strategy, and it cannot tell me whether reranking earns its latency. By the time
I built the eval harness afterwards I would be fitting it to the configuration I
had already chosen.

**Evaluate informally.** Keep a list of twenty questions and check them by hand
after changes. This is what I would actually have done, and it degrades the first
week something urgent comes up.

sections.heading: Consequences
sections.content:
The visible part of the project is the last part finished, so for several weeks
the site has a chat box that cannot answer anything. I have written that on the
page rather than faking it, which is its own small test of the principle.

What it buys: when the ablation table is finished, every row is a real run on the
same golden set, and the shipping configuration is chosen on evidence. I will be
able to say what hybrid retrieval bought over pure vector search on my own data,
whether the reranker justified its latency, and where the relevance threshold
came from. Those are the questions an AI engineering interview actually asks, and
the answer "it felt better" fails all of them.

The risk I am carrying is that the measurement work is slower and less motivating
than the interface work, and an unfinished eval harness with no chat box is worth
nothing at all. The mitigation is the phase gate: one phase per session, reviewed
and committed, so the thing is always in a state I could show.

These are my own answers, written down so that what the assistant says and what I
say in a room are the same thing.

## Why move from IT support to AI and ML engineering?

Two things, and the second one matters more.

I had been studying through the IIIT Bangalore Data Science programme alongside
the Capgemini job, finishing with the NLP specialisation in October 2025, so the
interest was two years old rather than a sudden decision.

The part that actually moved me was what I kept seeing in the queue. Problems
that took days to resolve by hand were problems a system could solve, and I
started wanting to build those systems instead of working around them. The access
request tool I built was the first time I did it, and the work felt completely
different from operating someone else's software. My dissertation is on agentic
AI and LLMs, which is the same instinct with better tools behind it.

## What ML have you actually shipped, end to end?

Nothing in a production role, and I would rather say that first than have you
find it.

What I have shipped end to end: a Python tool at Capgemini that used a language
model to turn prose access requests into concrete directory changes for my
approval, which ran daily and saved me 2 to 5 hours a week. Two analysis projects
on real datasets of 175,777 and 3,014,248 rows, with the metrics published and
the mistakes in them documented. And this assistant, which is a retrieval
pipeline with an eval harness that gates the deploy, built in the open.

That is the honest answer. The system is public, so you can check it rather than
take my word for it.

sections.heading: Three years of IT support. What does that give you that a CS graduate doesn't?
sections.content:
I have been on the receiving end of bad systems. Fifty incidents a day is a
feedback loop on what actually breaks in production and why, and most people
coming straight out of a degree have never had to support software they did not
write.

The more useful half is what that turns into. Sitting in that queue is where I
started seeing which problems were worth automating: the ones that took days to
fix by hand and should have taken minutes. That is what pushed me toward building
agents rather than scripts, and it is a sense of what is worth building that is
hard to get from coursework.

## Walk me through a model you built and what went wrong with it.

The delivery-time regression. 175,777 orders, predicting delivery duration from
the order and the state of the courier fleet.

The brief pointed at Recursive Feature Elimination as a refinement step, so I ran
it, cut 12 features to 8, and reported the result. All 12 features scored test R²
0.8800. The 8 RFE features scored 0.8191. Feature elimination made it measurably
worse and I did not notice at the time, because I treated RFE as a step you apply
rather than a choice you test.

There is a second layer to it. The scaled run scored 0.8737, and I would once
have said scaling helped. It cannot: ordinary least squares is scale-invariant,
so R² cannot change. The real cause is that RFE selected a different set of eight
features on the scaled matrix, swapping a weekend flag for a second courier-load
count. The lesson I took is that a result needs an explanation before it is a
result, and I had an unexplained six-point gap sitting in my notebook for a year.

sections.heading: You're mid-MSc. How would you handle a role alongside study?
sections.content:
I did exactly this for two years. The IIIT Bangalore programme ran alongside a
full-time Senior Analyst role at Capgemini and finished in October 2025, while I
was still handling the daily incident queue.

So it is evidence rather than a promise. My visa permits 20 hours a week in term
time and full time during university holidays, and I would rather agree a
schedule that fits inside that than over-commit and miss on both sides.

## Why did Capgemini end in December 2025?

I resigned to move to London and start the MSc. Last working day was 18 December
2025, and the relieving letter says resignation. Clean break, good terms, and I
would work with that team again.

## What are you weakest at right now?

Deep learning frameworks. PyTorch and TensorFlow are marked `familiar` on my own
profile, and that is accurate: coursework and tutorials, no trained model in
production or in a public repository. If you need someone who can pick up an
existing training loop and debug it on day one, that is not me yet.

I am not going to dress that up, partly because the whole premise of this project
is that claims come with evidence, and partly because an inflated answer here
collapses on the first follow-up question. What I would point at instead is that
every level on my profile is set this way, so the rows that say `strong` mean it.

The fix is the obvious one and it is in progress: the stretch work on this system
includes training a scope classifier and a small embedding adapter, which turns
that row into something with a model card behind it rather than a claim.

chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt discusses the results of a linear regression model for predicting delivery time, comparing models with all features, with recursive feature elimination (RFE) on unscaled data, and with RFE on scaled data, and explains why scaling changed the feature selection and affected performance.

chunks.content:
Fit a gradient-boosted baseline alongside it. Not to submit, but to find out what the linear
assumption cost. Without that number I cannot say whether R² 0.88 is good or whether a tree
model would have reached 0.95 on the same features, and that is the first thing anyone
technical will ask. The brief fixing the model is a reason I did not do it during the
assignment, not a reason it should stay undone.

I would also stop treating RFE as a step you apply. On this data it needed a sweep across
feature counts with the scores plotted, which would have shown the drop immediately instead of
leaving me to find it a year later.

## Correction

The written answers in the submitted notebook describe a different dataset. They name columns
such as `Discount_offered`, `Weight_in_gms` and `Warehouse_block`, which belong to a retail
shipping dataset and do not appear in this data, and one answer still carries a "replace with
the actual column name" placeholder. The code and the metrics are sound. The prose on top of
them was not reviewed, and it is being rewritten against the actual heatmap and coefficient
output.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt discusses the decision to fit a gradient‑boosted baseline to evaluate the linear regression assumption and the shortcomings of using recursive feature elimination without a sweep, in the context of a delivery time prediction case study. It also notes that the original notebook’s prose referenced a different retail shipping dataset and is being rewritten to match the actual heatmap and coefficient output.

chunks.content:
Work out when and where New York taxi demand actually is, from the city's own 2023 yellow cab
trip records, and turn that into something a dispatcher could act on. A single month of those
records is 3,014,248 trips across 22 columns, so the first problem is that the data does not
fit comfortably in memory on a laptop.

## Constraints

A graded assignment on the IIIT Bangalore programme, with a stated target of keeping the
working set near 250,000 to 300,000 rows. Local machine, no cluster. That forced the sampling
decision up front rather than letting me defer it.

## What I did

I sampled across all twelve months of 2023 rather than taking one month whole, which keeps
seasonal variation in the data, and landed at 489,542 trips. Then the cleaning, which took
longer than the analysis:

- Dropped `vendorid` and `store_and_fwd_flag` as unusable for the questions I had.
- Investigated negative fares before removing them, broken down by rate code, because a
  negative fare is usually a refund rather than an error and I wanted to know which.
- Filtered zero and negative values across fare, tip, total and distance.
- Bounded trip duration to between 1 and 180 minutes, distance to under 50 miles, and
  passenger count to 1 to 6. Each of those cut a tail that would otherwise have dominated the
  averages.
- Joined the trips to the city's taxi zone shapefile through `LocationID` so pickups and
  dropoffs became places rather than integers.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt describes the initial data preparation steps for a case study on optimizing NYC taxi dispatch, including sampling 2023 trip records, cleaning fields, filtering outliers, and joining zone shapefiles. It is part of a larger project titled “What 490,000 New York taxi trips say about when drivers actually earn.”

chunks.content:
**Tipping is about when and how, not how far.** Tip percentages are highest between 10pm and
2am, and card payments tip substantially more than cash. That is the finding I would lead
with, because it points at driver earnings rather than company revenue, and the action it
implies costs nothing: a driver choosing between a late shift and an early one has a reason to
pick the late one.

Demand moves through the day in a shape a dispatcher can use. Mornings load from the outer
residential zones into Midtown and the Financial District; evenings reverse it; late Friday and
Saturday nights concentrate in the nightlife zones; the 3am to 6am window is airport traffic
and shift workers. The top ten pickup and dropoff zones, the pickup-to-dropoff ratio per zone,
and night-hour pickup concentration are all computed directly from the trip records.

Fare per mile is not flat. Comparing vendors across three distance tiers, under 2 miles, 2 to 5,
and over 5, short trips earn far more per mile than long ones, which is what you would expect
from a fixed base fare and why long airport runs are less attractive than they look.

## What I would do differently

**Three figures in my submitted notebook are plotted from random numbers.** The starter template
seeded the zone trip counts with `np.random.randint(0, 100, len(zones))` and the route speeds
with `np.random.uniform(20, 60, ...)` as scaffolding to demonstrate the plotting calls, and I
never replaced them with real counts. A later cell then divides those random numbers by the
sampling fraction to "scale up to the full population", which scales up noise. So the trips-per-
zone choropleth and the slowest-routes analysis carry no information, and the congestion
recommendation that depended on them is withdrawn. The zone findings above come from the
value-count work, which is real. I found this on review, months after submitting, and it is the
most useful thing this project taught me: a figure that renders is not a figure that is right.

My two conclusion cells also contradict each other on peak hours, one saying 1pm to 9pm and the
other 7am to 9am and 5pm to 7pm. I did not reconcile them at the time, which means at least one
was written from impression rather than from the plot.

The conclusions themselves sit inside triple-quoted strings in code cells, so they do not render
as text. The best part of the work is nearly invisible to anyone reading the notebook.

And the recommendations need numbers. "Raise peak fares 10 to 15%" is an opinion until it comes
with an estimated revenue effect, and the data could have supported that estimate. A
recommendation without a number is not an analysis result.

Finally, I would test whether the filtering shaped the findings. Removing trips over 180 minutes
and over 50 miles is defensible, but those are exactly the trips that matter most to a driver
deciding whether to take an airport run. I should have run the headline findings once with the
bounds and once without and reported whether they held.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt discusses tipping patterns, demand timing, fare per mile variations, and methodological issues in a case study on 490,000 New York taxi trips, highlighting how driver earnings and dispatch decisions can be informed by the data.

chunks.content:
Access requests arrived as prose in ServiceNow tickets: create this account, add
this person to that group, revoke this permission. Reading the ticket and working
out which concrete directory change it was asking for took most of the time. The
change itself took seconds.

A language model is good at exactly that translation step, and I had an internal
one available. The question was how much authority to give it.

## Decision

The model proposes, I approve, the script applies. The model never touched the
directory directly.

## Alternatives considered

**Unattended end to end.** The script reads the ticket, decides, and makes the
change. This saves the most time and I rejected it. Directory writes are
destructive and audited, and a wrong group removal locks someone out of their job
with no clean undo. I would also have had no answer if it had gone wrong once.

**Rules and regular expressions, no model.** Fails on the actual problem. People
describe access requests in wildly inconsistent prose, and a rule set broad enough
to cover that variation becomes a worse language model.

## Consequences

It saved 2 to 5 hours a week of my own time, which was the interpretation step
rather than the approval step. I stayed accountable for every change, which was
the point.

What I did not see at the time: the approval step was a free labelled dataset. I
saw every proposal next to what I actually applied, every day, and logged none of
it. With that log I could have reported an acceptance rate, found which request
types it misread, and answered "could this run unattended?" with evidence instead
of instinct. I was shipping a model with no eval set, before I knew that was the
name for the mistake.
chunks.contextBlurb: The decision document explains how Capgemini implemented a human‑in‑the‑loop approval step for language‑model‑generated scripts that modify Active Directory, describing the problem of interpreting prose access requests, the chosen approach, alternatives considered, and the resulting time savings and accountability.

chunks.content:
By 2025 I was a Senior Analyst at Capgemini, two and a half years in, running 50
or more incidents a day against SLA and administering Active Directory and
endpoint compliance across enterprise environments. The role was stable and I was
good at it.

Two things had changed underneath that. I had been studying through the IIIT
Bangalore Data Science programme alongside the job, which finished with the NLP
specialisation in October 2025, so the interest was two years old rather than
sudden. And I had built the access-request tool described in
[001](001-human-approval-before-directory-writes.md). That tool was the first
time the work felt like engineering a system rather than operating one, and I
wanted considerably more of that than the role contained.

## Decision

Resign in December 2025 and move to London for an MSc in Artificial Intelligence
and Computer Science at Northeastern University London.

## Alternatives considered

**Stay and move internally.** Capgemini is large and has ML work in it. The
honest reason I did not pursue this: internal moves from operations into
engineering are slow and usually need the credential I did not have. I would have
spent two years waiting for permission.

**Keep studying part time and stay employed.** Cheaper and lower risk, and it is
what I had already been doing for two years. It had produced certificates rather
than shipped systems, which told me the constraint was time and not motivation.

**Self-study and apply directly.** No tuition, no visa cost, no relocation. I
rejected it because I had no production ML to point at, and without either a
credential or a portfolio the applications go nowhere. The MSc buys the
credential; this assistant is meant to be the portfolio half.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt explains the author’s decision to resign from a stable senior analyst role at Capgemini in December 2025 to pursue an MSc in Artificial Intelligence and Computer Science at Northeastern University London, after realizing that their interest in data science had grown over two years and they wanted more engineering work than their current operations position offered.

chunks.content:
The cost is real: a salary given up, tuition, and a student visa that permits
20 hours a week in term time rather than full-time work until the course
completes in May 2027.

What it buys is time to build things that can be measured, and a dissertation in
agentic AI and LLMs that sits on the same ground as the work I want to be hired
for. The thing I am still exposed to is the obvious one: three years of
production operations is not three years of production ML, and I say so rather
than blur it.
chunks.contextBlurb: In the decision document “Leave a senior IT operations role for an MSc in AI” by Capgemini, the author explains the financial and time costs of leaving a senior IT operations position to pursue an MSc in AI, noting the trade‑off between salary, tuition, and a part‑time work visa, while highlighting the opportunity to develop measurable projects and a dissertation on agentic AI and LLMs that aligns with future hiring goals.

chunks.content:
This assistant is a retrieval system with a chat box on the front. The chat box
is the part anyone can see and the part I most wanted to build. The retrieval
quality is the part that decides whether anything it says is true.

The phase order I am following puts corpus and ingestion first, then a retrieval
pipeline where every option is a config flag, then the eval harness, then an
ablation study across those flags, and only then the chat interface. Chat is
phase five of ten.

## Decision

No chat interface until the golden set, the retrieval metrics and the
faithfulness judge exist and produce numbers.

## Alternatives considered

**Chat first, evaluate later.** The natural order, and the one I wanted. It fails
for a specific reason rather than a moral one: once a chat UI exists, retrieval
gets tuned by asking it questions and seeing whether the answers feel right.
Feeling right is not a measurement, it does not survive a change to the chunking
strategy, and it cannot tell me whether reranking earns its latency. By the time
I built the eval harness afterwards I would be fitting it to the configuration I
had already chosen.

**Evaluate informally.** Keep a list of twenty questions and check them by hand
after changes. This is what I would actually have done, and it degrades the first
week something urgent comes up.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt is from the decision document “Build the eval harness before the chat interface” for the This assistant project, describing the planned order of development phases and the decision to postpone the chat interface until retrieval metrics and a faithfulness judge are established.

chunks.content:
The visible part of the project is the last part finished, so for several weeks
the site has a chat box that cannot answer anything. I have written that on the
page rather than faking it, which is its own small test of the principle.

What it buys: when the ablation table is finished, every row is a real run on the
same golden set, and the shipping configuration is chosen on evidence. I will be
able to say what hybrid retrieval bought over pure vector search on my own data,
whether the reranker justified its latency, and where the relevance threshold
came from. Those are the questions an AI engineering interview actually asks, and
the answer "it felt better" fails all of them.

The risk I am carrying is that the measurement work is slower and less motivating
than the interface work, and an unfinished eval harness with no chat box is worth
nothing at all. The mitigation is the phase gate: one phase per session, reviewed
and committed, so the thing is always in a state I could show.
chunks.contextBlurb: This excerpt appears in a decision document for the This assistant project, where the author explains that they are prioritizing the construction of an evaluation harness before developing the chat interface, arguing that having a complete ablation table and measurable evidence of performance is more valuable than a partially functional chat box.

chunks.content:
These are my own answers, written down so that what the assistant says and what I
say in a room are the same thing.

## Why move from IT support to AI and ML engineering?

Two things, and the second one matters more.

I had been studying through the IIIT Bangalore Data Science programme alongside
the Capgemini job, finishing with the NLP specialisation in October 2025, so the
interest was two years old rather than a sudden decision.

The part that actually moved me was what I kept seeing in the queue. Problems
that took days to resolve by hand were problems a system could solve, and I
started wanting to build those systems instead of working around them. The access
request tool I built was the first time I did it, and the work felt completely
different from operating someone else's software. My dissertation is on agentic
AI and LLMs, which is the same instinct with better tools behind it.

## What ML have you actually shipped, end to end?

Nothing in a production role, and I would rather say that first than have you
find it.

What I have shipped end to end: a Python tool at Capgemini that used a language
model to turn prose access requests into concrete directory changes for my
approval, which ran daily and saved me 2 to 5 hours a week. Two analysis projects
on real datasets of 175,777 and 3,014,248 rows, with the metrics published and
the mistakes in them documented. And this assistant, which is a retrieval
pipeline with an eval harness that gates the deploy, built in the open.

That is the honest answer. The system is public, so you can check it rather than
take my word for it.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt is from an interview where the author explains why they transitioned from IT support to AI and ML engineering, highlighting their data science studies and a desire to automate repetitive tasks, and then candidly discusses the ML projects they have shipped, including a Python tool that automates directory changes and a retrieval‑based assistant.

chunks.content:
I have been on the receiving end of bad systems. Fifty incidents a day is a
feedback loop on what actually breaks in production and why, and most people
coming straight out of a degree have never had to support software they did not
write.

The more useful half is what that turns into. Sitting in that queue is where I
started seeing which problems were worth automating: the ones that took days to
fix by hand and should have taken minutes. That is what pushed me toward building
agents rather than scripts, and it is a sense of what is worth building that is
hard to get from coursework.

## Walk me through a model you built and what went wrong with it.

The delivery-time regression. 175,777 orders, predicting delivery duration from
the order and the state of the courier fleet.

The brief pointed at Recursive Feature Elimination as a refinement step, so I ran
it, cut 12 features to 8, and reported the result. All 12 features scored test R²
0.8800. The 8 RFE features scored 0.8191. Feature elimination made it measurably
worse and I did not notice at the time, because I treated RFE as a step you apply
rather than a choice you test.

There is a second layer to it. The scaled run scored 0.8737, and I would once
have said scaling helped. It cannot: ordinary least squares is scale-invariant,
so R² cannot change. The real cause is that RFE selected a different set of eight
features on the scaled matrix, swapping a weekend flag for a second courier-load
count. The lesson I took is that a result needs an explanation before it is a
result, and I had an unexplained six-point gap sitting in my notebook for a year.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt comes from an interview where the author explains how daily exposure to production incidents revealed the need for automation, leading them to build agents instead of scripts, and then discusses a specific modeling mistake involving Recursive Feature Elimination and scaling in a delivery-time regression project.

chunks.content:
I did exactly this for two years. The IIIT Bangalore programme ran alongside a
full-time Senior Analyst role at Capgemini and finished in October 2025, while I
was still handling the daily incident queue.

So it is evidence rather than a promise. My visa permits 20 hours a week in term
time and full time during university holidays, and I would rather agree a
schedule that fits inside that than over-commit and miss on both sides.

## Why did Capgemini end in December 2025?

I resigned to move to London and start the MSc. Last working day was 18 December
2025, and the relieving letter says resignation. Clean break, good terms, and I
would work with that team again.

## What are you weakest at right now?

Deep learning frameworks. PyTorch and TensorFlow are marked `familiar` on my own
profile, and that is accurate: coursework and tutorials, no trained model in
production or in a public repository. If you need someone who can pick up an
existing training loop and debug it on day one, that is not me yet.

I am not going to dress that up, partly because the whole premise of this project
is that claims come with evidence, and partly because an inflated answer here
collapses on the first follow-up question. What I would point at instead is that
every level on my profile is set this way, so the rows that say `strong` mean it.

The fix is the obvious one and it is in progress: the stretch work on this system
includes training a scope classifier and a small embedding adapter, which turns
that row into something with a model card behind it rather than a claim.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt is from an interview answer where the speaker explains how they balanced a full‑time analyst role at Capgemini with a two‑year IIIT Bangalore programme, clarifies their visa‑limited work hours, and discusses their resignation in December 2025 to pursue an MSc in London.
